title: Albania: Europe’s Best-Value Coastline Before It Gets Busy
metaDescription: A complete guide to travelling in Albania — the Riviera, the mountains, Ottoman towns, costs, transport and when to go.
excerpt: Ionian water, Ottoman towns, alpine valleys and prices half of Greece. Albania is having its moment, and the moment is not over yet.
author: Trypinn Team
content:
The water off Ksamil is the same Ionian Sea that laps Corfu, twenty minutes away across the strait. The mountains behind the coast road are the same range that runs down through Greece. The Ottoman-era stone towns are as complete as anything in the Balkans.

What is different is the price, and the number of people.

Albania spent most of the twentieth century closed off, which is precisely why its coastline was never developed into the wall of concrete that swallowed stretches of Spain and Croatia. It is developing now, quickly, and the honest framing is this: **go soon, and go with the understanding that "undiscovered" stopped being accurate around 2023.**

## When to Go

- **May to mid-June** — the best window. Warm, green, quiet, everything open
- **July and August** — hot, and genuinely busy on the Riviera. Ksamil in August is not a secret beach
- **September to mid-October** — arguably the best of all. The sea is at its warmest, the crowds have gone, prices drop
- **November to April** — the coast largely closes, but the mountains and cities are atmospheric and very cheap

## The Albanian Riviera

The coast road from Vlorë south to Sarandë is the trip's spine, and one of the great drives in Europe. It climbs over the **Llogara Pass** — a genuinely spectacular ascent through pine forest to a viewpoint where the mountains drop straight into the Ionian — then descends to a string of coastal villages.

**Dhërmi and Drymades** — the best balance of beach quality and atmosphere. Clear water, pebble beaches, a growing but not overwhelming bar scene.

**Himarë** — a proper town rather than a resort, with a Greek-speaking minority, an old castle quarter on the hill and good seafood.

**Gjipe Beach** — reached by a canyon walk or by boat. Worth the effort, and the effort is what keeps it manageable.

**Ksamil** — the famous one, with the turquoise water and the small islands. Extremely busy in summer, and the beach is now almost entirely covered in rented sunbeds. Go in June or late September, or go early in the morning.

**Sarandë** — the southern hub. Functional rather than beautiful, useful as a base, and the ferry port for Corfu.

![Albania travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1632902346990-4550c46a2314?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Beyond the Beach

This is where Albania becomes a genuinely interesting country rather than a cheap coastline.

**Berat** — the "city of a thousand windows", a UNESCO-listed Ottoman town of white houses stacked up a hillside beneath a castle that still has people living inside its walls. One of the most beautiful towns in the Balkans.

**Gjirokastër** — the other Ottoman town, stone-roofed and steep, with a vast castle and a distinctive, slightly severe beauty. Between them, Berat and Gjirokastër justify the trip on their own.

**Butrint** — an archaeological site near Sarandë layered with Greek, Roman, Byzantine and Venetian remains, in a lagoon setting. Genuinely impressive and usually quiet.

**The Blue Eye (Syri i Kaltër)** — a karst spring of improbable blue. Busy, brief, and worth the stop en route.

**Theth and the Albanian Alps** — the country's other great landscape. The Theth-to-Valbona hike is a full day over a pass between two remote valleys, with guesthouses at each end, and it is one of the best day hikes in Europe. Reaching Valbona involves a ferry across Lake Koman through a flooded gorge, which is itself a highlight.

**Tirana** — the capital, transformed over the last two decades. Brightly painted apartment blocks, a good coffee culture, Bunk'Art's Cold War bunker museums, and the Blloku district. Two days is plenty and they are two good days.

![Albania travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1502824420498-012d4c4f0c42?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Getting Around

**Renting a car is strongly recommended.** The coast road and the interior are not well served by public transport, and the freedom to stop matters here more than in most countries.

Caveats worth knowing: Albanian driving is assertive, roads vary from excellent new highway to broken mountain track, and mountain roads to places like Theth require care and ideally higher clearance. Petrol stations are sparse in the interior — fill up when you can.

Without a car, **furgon** minibuses connect most towns. They are cheap, informal, leave when full, and require patience and a phrasebook.

Ferries connect Sarandë to Corfu in about half an hour, which makes combining Albania and Greece straightforward.

## What It Costs

Among the best value in Europe:

- **Budget** — $35–50 per day
- **Mid-range** — $70–110
- **Comfortable** — $150–250

A good guesthouse room in Berat or Gjirokastër costs a fraction of its Croatian equivalent. Seafood dinners with wine on the Riviera cost what a starter costs in Italy. Car rental is inexpensive. The exception is peak-season Ksamil accommodation, which has risen sharply.

## Practicalities

- **Currency** — the Albanian lek. Euros are accepted in tourist areas at a poor rate. Withdraw lek from an ATM
- **Cash** — essential outside cities. Many guesthouses, restaurants and all furgons are cash-only
- **Visas** — visa-free for most nationalities, including many that need a Schengen visa for the EU. Albania sits outside Schengen, so days here do not count against your 90/180 allowance, which makes it useful for long European trips
- **Language** — Albanian, with Italian and increasingly English widely understood. Greek in the south
- **Safety** — very safe for travellers. The country's old reputation is decades out of date

## A Ten-Day Route

- **Days 1–2** — Tirana
- **Day 3** — Berat
- **Days 4–5** — Gjirokastër and Blue Eye
- **Days 6–8** — the Riviera: Himarë, Dhërmi, Gjipe, Butrint, Ksamil
- **Days 9–10** — north to Shkodër, Lake Koman ferry and Theth if you have the time and the legs

Reverse it if you are flying into Corfu and ferrying across.

## The Honest Caveats

- **Ksamil in August** is genuinely crowded and largely privatised by sunbed operators. Manage expectations or go in shoulder season
- **Construction is everywhere** along the coast. Some of it will be beautiful and some of it will not
- **Rubbish** remains a visible problem in places, and it is jarring against the landscape
- **Infrastructure varies enormously.** A new highway can become a gravel track without warning
- **Tourism has grown very fast**, and service quality has not always kept up

None of these are reasons not to go. They are reasons to go with realistic expectations and a rental car.

Albania rewards a loose plan more than a fixed one — the coast road is full of unmarked turnings toward beaches that are not on any list. Map the fixed points, leave the rest open, and if you are travelling with others, agree in advance that the itinerary is a suggestion. Putting the route and the bookable items into a shared plan on **Trypinn** and leaving the days between them deliberately blank is exactly the right shape for this trip.
